title: Margin and capital
text: A trading firm's positions are limited by more than its own risk limits. Margin decides how much it must post against each position. Capital rules decide how much loss the firm itself must be able to absorb.

title: Why it matters
text: Margin protects the lender or clearing house from the trader. Capital protects customers and the market from the firm. When either runs short, positions get cut, often at the worst moment. Both are written as rules with numbers, so a trading system can compute them before it trades.

title: Margin
text: In US stocks, the Federal Reserve's Regulation T sets initial margin at 50 percent of a position's market value. FINRA Rule 4210 then sets maintenance margin at 25 percent for long positions. Say you buy $100,000 of stock, with $50,000 of your own and $50,000 borrowed. Your equity must stay at 25 percent of the value. That fails once the position falls below about $66,700, a drop of a third, and a margin call follows. Futures margin works differently: the clearing house sets it per contract, from its risk models.

title: Net capital
text: A US broker-dealer must keep net capital under SEC Rule 15c3-1. A dealer needs at least $100,000, and a firm carrying customer accounts at least $250,000. Its own positions are haircut. For most stocks, the haircut is 15 percent of the larger of the long or short side. Hold $10 million of stock and $1.5 million comes off your net worth before it counts as capital. A hedged book is cut on its larger side only, up to a point.

title: The EU regime
text: In the EU, the Investment Firms Regulation has applied since 26 June 2021. A firm dealing on its own account needs initial capital of 750,000 euros. Its ongoing requirement is the highest of three numbers: a permanent minimum, a quarter of its annual fixed overheads, and K-factors. K-factors scale with the risk the firm poses to clients, to markets, and to itself.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's limits are where these numbers would plug in. Pre-trade risk caps any position at 2,000 shares, counting every working order. At $50 a share, that is $100,000 at most, per symbol. Under Regulation T that full position needs $50,000 of margin. As a dealer's own position, its haircut would be $15,000. These are illustrations, but they show why limits are set in money, not just shares.

title: Takeaway
text: So what do pros do? They compute margin and capital before they trade, as limits, not as a report the next morning. They keep a buffer above every minimum. They stress test for clearing houses raising margin on a volatile day. And they watch gross positions, not just net. This is education, not legal advice.
